title: The Cost of Keeping China Out
gist: Cowhey and Rithmire argue (in an essay cut short by a paywall) that Washington's fear-driven exclusion of Chinese investment and products — especially EVs, now effectively absent from the U.S. market despite winning over consumers from London to Santiago — is hurting American competitiveness rather than protecting it.

themes.theme: China's visible lead in frontier commercial tech

insights.claim: Travelers returning from China commonly report having seen a technological future not yet visible to most Americans: robots that make and serve restaurant food, drones delivering food and medicine, and industrial and humanoid robots deployed on factory floors.
insights.speaker: Peter Cowhey
insights.so_what: Suggests China's frontier commercial-tech deployment (robotics, autonomous delivery) has outpaced visible U.S. deployment, a signal worth tracking for competitive positioning in robotics and automation sectors.
insights.quote: The country’s advances in frontier commercial technologies are visible in the robots that make and serve food in restaurants; the drones that deliver food and medicine; and the deployment of industrial and humanoid robots on factory floors.

insights.claim: Chinese electric vehicles — offered at affordable prices with features like swappable batteries and massage chairs — have won over consumers in markets ranging from London to Santiago, even as they remain effectively absent from the U.S. market.
insights.speaker: Peter Cowhey
insights.so_what: Highlights a stark U.S.-market exception to Chinese EV global market penetration, likely driven by tariffs/investment restrictions — relevant for assessing the durability of that policy wall against future trade or political shifts.
insights.quote: Even outside China, most of the world is now familiar with Chinese electric vehicles that are as affordable as they are sleek, with massage chairs and swappable batteries winning over passengers from London to Santiago.

insights.claim: Most Americans are unaware of China's frontier-technology advances because Chinese EVs are effectively absent from the U.S. market, unlike in most of the rest of the world.
insights.speaker: Peter Cowhey
insights.so_what: Implies a growing perception gap between U.S. policymakers/consumers and the actual pace of Chinese technological advance, which could lead to policy miscalibration on China competitiveness measures.
insights.quote: Most Americans, however, are unaware of this future. Chinese EVs are effectively absent from the U.S.
insights.locator: paragraph transitioning to U.S. market absence

themes.theme: The central thesis: exclusion has a competitiveness cost

insights.claim: The authors argue that Washington's fear of Chinese investment — manifested in policies that keep Chinese capital and products like EVs out of the U.S. market — is actively hurting American competitiveness rather than protecting it.
insights.speaker: Peter Cowhey
insights.so_what: A contrarian framing relevant to debates on U.S.-China investment screening and tariff policy: the piece argues protectionist exclusion carries a real, underappreciated competitiveness cost that should factor into policy cost-benefit analysis.
insights.locator: article subtitle: 'How Washington's Fear of Chinese Investment Hurts American Competitiveness'
